Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Imani finds it hardest in the quiet hours before dawn, mending nets on the deck of her boat. In the stillness, with the smell of salt and diesel in the air, the thoughts come loudest. It has been nearly a year since the accident, but the memory plays on a relentless loop, each detail sharp and punishing. It had started over something trivial, a disagreement about money for a new engine part. The argument had escalated, her voice rising with a frustration she now couldn't comprehend. Her husband, David, had grabbed his keys, his face a mask of hurt and anger, and slammed the door. Imani had stood in the kitchen, her own anger warring with a sudden, sharp regret. She was about to call out to him when she heard the screech of tires and the sickening, final sound of metal tearing into metal at the intersection just down their street.

In the months that followed, Imani constructed a life around avoiding the memory. She learned that the world was filled with ambushes. A news report showing a crumpled car would send a jolt of ice through her veins, her heart hammering against her ribs so hard she’d feel dizzy. She’d have to grip the counter, convinced she was about to collapse. At the docks, when the other fishermen would casually mention a fender-bender or a close call on the highway, a hot, uncontrollable rage would surge through her. She once snapped at a colleague so fiercely for telling a story about a traffic jam that he didn't speak to her for a week. She had come to believe these strong feelings were dangerous, that the guilt and horror were a poison that could overwhelm and destroy her if she let them in. So she fought to keep them out.

Her nights became a strategic battle against her own mind. Sleep was an enemy, a quiet space where the intrusive thoughts could corner her. She would stay up until two or three in the morning, watching mindless television or scrolling through shopping websites on her phone. Packages began arriving almost daily—expensive fishing lures she didn’t need, clothes she would never wear. The brief thrill of the purchase was a fleeting distraction, a momentary silence in the storm of self-recrimination. During the day, she filled any silence with activity, but when alone, she would find herself lost in endless, agonizing revisions of the past. She would dwell for hours on how the event could have been prevented, replaying the argument, changing her words, imagining herself calling him back from the door. Each mental simulation ended in the same place: a crushing certainty that it was her fault. The accident happened because of the way she acted.

The belief has settled deep into her bones, a truth more real than any other. She had failed to protect him. This conviction governed everything. When David, who had thankfully recovered after months of physical therapy, would reach for her hand, she would see not her husband but her own catastrophic failure. The guilt was a physical barrier between them, making her irritable and distant. She felt she didn’t deserve his kindness or forgiveness. The upcoming one-year anniversary of the crash looms like a tidal wave she is certain will drown her. It was David who finally insisted she seek help, after finding a credit card statement showing thousands of dollars in impulsive late-night purchases. He didn’t yell. He simply sat beside her and said, “I survived the crash, Imani. But I’m afraid I’m losing you now.” Imani is here because she is terrified he is right, but an even greater terror paralyzes her: the fear that she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened, and that she will have to live with this feeling forever.
